title: LAMECH TOOK TWO WIVES: The Bible’s First Polygamist Appears Only Generations After Eden
paragraphs: LAMECH TOOK TWO WIVES: The Bible’s First Polygamist Appears Only Generations After Eden
Eden had barely disappeared behind humanity when one quiet sentence revealed just how quickly the human heart could begin rewriting what God had made.
There are verses in the Bible that announce catastrophe with thunder.
And then there are verses that whisper it.
Genesis 4:19 is one of those whispers.
No voice from heaven interrupting the scene.
Just one sentence buried inside a genealogy:
“And Lamech took unto him two wives…”
Because by the time you reach that sentence, humanity is only a few generations removed from Eden.
Adam had known what it was like to hear the voice of God in a world untouched by human sin.
Eve had known what it was like to live before shame.
They had also known the terrible moment when everything fractured.
Then their son Cain murdered his brother Abel.
And now, several generations into Cain’s line, Scripture introduces a man named Lamech.
And suddenly there are two wives.
The Hebrew refuses to soften it:
Their names were Adah and Zillah.
This matters because Genesis has already shown us something different.
Before sin entered the world, God did not bring Adam a collection of women.
And centuries later, when Jesus Christ was questioned about marriage, He did something incredibly important.
Jesus went all the way back to creation.
He pointed to the beginning and declared that the Creator made them male and female, and that the man would be joined to his wife so that “the two” would become “one flesh.”
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Because Scripture records many things it does not thereby endorse.
The Bible is brutally honest about human beings.
The Bible does not airbrush its heroes because Scripture is not propaganda for human greatness.
It is revelation of God's holiness, humanity's sin, and ultimately our desperate need for redemption.
So when Genesis says Lamech took two wives, we should not read description as command.
“And God commanded Lamech to take two wives.”
It simply tells us what happened.
And where it happens in the story is haunting.
Because Genesis 4 is showing us what humanity can become when sin is allowed to travel.
Cain's sin did not remain in a field beside Abel's body.
Sin never stays politely where we leave it.
It enters our definition of normal.
That is one of the terrifying lessons of Genesis 4.
Yesterday's rebellion can become tomorrow's tradition.
Yesterday's scandal can become tomorrow's normal.
And eventually people can inherit something broken without even remembering what wholeness looked like.
Maybe that is why Lamech's story feels disturbingly modern.
Because we know how quickly human beings learn to rename things.
And sometimes we become so accustomed to our own darkness that we stop asking whether the thing we have normalized was ever God's design.
Because Genesis does not merely tell us about his marriages.
It lets us hear him speak.
And what comes out of his mouth sounds like the soundtrack of a civilization learning to glorify itself.
“Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech…”
The wording has generated discussion concerning precisely how Lamech's statement should be understood, but the violent boast at the center of the poem is unmistakable.
“If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.”
Yet even in judgment, God placed a protective mark upon him so that vengeance would not spiral endlessly.
But generations later, Lamech takes the language of vengeance and magnifies it.
The language has moved from divine restraint surrounding Cain to human boasting on Lamech's lips.
Power has become something to brag about.
And suddenly Genesis 4 does not feel ancient anymore.
Because some of us have never killed anyone…
but we know exactly what it means to keep score.
We remember what our father said.
What that person took from us.
And somewhere inside, quietly, we write our own song of Lamech.
I'll make sure everybody knows what you did.
I'll make sure you regret losing me.
I'll carry it for twenty years.
But then Jesus enters the story.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because in Matthew 18, Peter asks Jesus how often he should forgive someone who sins against him.
Jesus answers with language that deliberately sounds startlingly familiar:
οὐ λέγω σοι ἕως ἑπτάκις ἀλλ᾽ ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά
The Greek is commonly rendered either “seventy-seven times” or “seventy times seven,” depending on translation and interpretation.
Either way, Christ's point is not that forgiveness should stop when somebody reaches a mathematical quota.
It is forgiveness refusing to live by the arithmetic of revenge.
And the echo back to Genesis 4 is difficult to miss.
Lamech says, in effect, “Look how severely I repay wounds.”
Jesus teaches His disciples, “Do not build your life around keeping score.”
Do you see what Jesus does?
He doesn't merely improve broken humanity.
Jesus did not come merely to make angry people slightly nicer.
He came to make dead people alive.
The wounded people who became people who wound others.
The people hiding behind smiles at church.
The people reading Christian posts while secretly wondering whether God could possibly still want them.
And perhaps this is where Lamech's story stops being about Lamech.
Because there may be something you have normalized that God has been trying to expose.
Something you have quietly told yourself:
Maybe anger runs through your family.
Maybe you learned as a child that love meant control.
Maybe nobody ever apologized in your home.
Maybe men were taught that repentance was weakness.
Maybe women were taught to tolerate what God never called good.
Maybe Scripture was used around you but Jesus was rarely reflected.
And now you are carrying wounds from people who were themselves carrying wounds.
That does not make sin harmless.
But it reminds us why humanity needs something far greater than behavior modification.
Because sin does not merely need management.
And that Savior has a name.
Genesis mentions livestock, music, bronze, and iron.
Human civilization advances technologically while the human heart remains desperately broken.
Human beings can become more sophisticated without becoming more holy.
We can build cities and still destroy families.
We can compose music while carrying hatred.
We can master metal while being mastered by sin.
We can put a computer in nearly every pocket on earth and still not know how to forgive the person sitting across the dinner table.
Genesis 4 does not end with Lamech.
After the violence, boasting, brokenness, and death, Scripture turns again toward Adam and Eve.
And Genesis 4 closes with these words:
“Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.”
What a way to end the chapter.
The chapter that contains murder does not end with murder.
The chapter that contains Lamech does not end with Lamech.
The chapter that shows humanity drifting farther from Eden ends with people calling upon the name of the LORD.
Not because humanity suddenly fixed itself.
But because God was not finished.
And God still wasn't finished when Noah came.
He wasn't finished when Abraham stumbled.
He wasn't finished when Jacob deceived.
He wasn't finished when Israel rebelled.
He wasn't finished when David fell.
He wasn't finished when Jerusalem wept.
He wasn't finished when prophets were rejected.
And He certainly wasn't finished when Jesus was nailed to a Roman cross.
Because what looked like humanity's greatest scandal became the stage upon which divine grace would be displayed.
At Calvary, Jesus did not answer human violence with greater human violence.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
And while Lamech's world sang the song of escalating vengeance, Jesus prayed over His executioners:
The Gospel does not tell you to pretend that nobody wounded you.
It tells you that your wound does not have to become your identity.
The Gospel does not say betrayal wasn't painful.
It says bitterness does not deserve the throne of your heart.
The Gospel does not tell you your past never happened.
It tells you your past does not get the final sentence.
Maybe your family story is ugly.
Jesus can meet you in truth.
Maybe you have committed sins you cannot imagine saying aloud.
Maybe you became the very person you promised yourself you would never become.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the grave.
The Greek word often translated repentance, μετάνοια — metanoia, carries the idea of a changed mind, a turning that reaches into the direction of life.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God today.
It is laying down your excuses.
And He does not save you because you cleaned yourself first.
The cross destroys both despair and pride because at the cross we discover two truths simultaneously:
Our sin was worse than we wanted to admit.
And God's grace is greater than we dared to believe.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message will always come back here.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle.
But sometimes three honest words are the beginning of stepping out of isolation.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, don't treat that as an excuse to condemn them.
Someone scrolling your profile tonight may be fighting a battle you know nothing about.
Someone may be one quiet moment away from giving up.
Someone may believe their scandal has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Come back when bitterness starts whispering again.
Come back when culture tells you that whatever feels normal must therefore be holy.
Come back when your past tells you that change is impossible.
Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered work is one practical way you can help biblical content continue reaching people who desperately need it.
Christ matters more than a brand.
And stay connected with Gospel Warrior.
Follow and invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever you have been quietly praying for.
Test what you read against God's Word.
And keep pointing people toward Jesus.
Because somewhere between Eden and Lamech, humanity demonstrated how quickly a broken heart can learn to call brokenness normal.
But somewhere between a manger and an empty tomb, God showed us something infinitely greater:
Brokenness does not have to be the end of the story.
Cain's line reminds us how sin can spread.
The cross shows us how far grace was willing to go to rescue sinners.
And the empty tomb declares that sin, shame, death, and the ugliest chapter of your life do not possess final authority over anyone who belongs to Christ.
So bring Him the chapter you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the family pattern you are terrified of repeating.
Bring Him the person you became while trying to survive what happened to you.
And discover that the Savior who already knows the whole story is still calling you toward Himself.
Your family's broken pattern may explain where the wound began—but Jesus Christ can decide where its reign ends.
